description: Creating and arranging figures and axes, controlling limits, ticks, labels, legends, colormaps and lighting, querying and setting graphics object properties, and saving or exporting figures to files. These functions turn a raw plot into a finished, publication-ready graphic.

tools.name: figure
tools.description: Creates a new figure window or makes an existing one current, and returns its handle. Properties set at creation control size, position, colour, visibility and name. Use it to start a fresh plot, to manage several plots at once, and to create invisible figures for headless batch rendering.
tools.usage:
figure
figure(n)
figure(f)
f = figure(Name, Value)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Figure number; creates or raises that figure.

parameters.name: 'Color', 'Name', 'NumberTitle'
parameters.description: Background colour and title bar options.

tools.notes: In `matlab -batch` runs, create figures with 'Visible','off' and export them; no window is shown but rendering still works. `figure(n)` with an integer reuses that numbered figure, which is handy in scripts.

tools.name: axes
tools.description: Creates a new axes object in the current figure at a specified position, or makes an existing axes current. Use it for custom layouts that `subplot` and `tiledlayout` cannot express, such as inset plots and overlapping axes. The returned handle can be passed as the first argument to plotting functions.
tools.usage:
axes
ax = axes
ax = axes(Name, Value)
axes(ax)

parameters.name: 'Position'
parameters.description: [left bottom width height] in normalized figure units.

parameters.name: 'Parent'
parameters.description: Figure, panel or layout that contains the axes.

tools.notes: Passing the axes handle explicitly to plotting functions is more robust than relying on the current axes, especially in callbacks and functions. `gca` returns the current axes.

tools.name: subplot
tools.description: Divides a figure into a grid of axes and makes one of them current, numbered row-wise from the top left. A subplot can span several grid cells when given a vector of indices. Use it for quick multi-panel figures; `tiledlayout` gives tighter spacing and more control in newer code.
tools.usage:
subplot(m, n, p)
subplot(m, n, p, 'replace')
subplot(m, n, [p1 p2])
ax = subplot(___)
subplot('Position', pos)

parameters.name: m, n
parameters.description: Number of rows and columns in the grid.

parameters.name: p
parameters.description: Index of the panel, counting across rows; a vector spans cells.

tools.notes: Calling subplot on a cell that already has axes deletes overlapping axes, which silently destroys plots when grids are mixed. `tiledlayout`/`nexttile` avoids that problem and wastes less white space.

tools.name: tiledlayout
tools.description: Creates a tiled chart layout for arranging multiple plots in a figure, with control over padding, tile spacing and whether the grid grows automatically. It supports shared titles and axis labels across all tiles. Use it in place of `subplot` for compact, well-aligned multi-panel figures.
tools.usage:
tiledlayout(m, n)
tiledlayout('flow')
t = tiledlayout(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: m, n
parameters.description: Grid size, or 'flow' to add tiles as needed.

tools.example:
t = tiledlayout(2, 2, 'TileSpacing', 'compact', 'Padding', 'compact');
nexttile; plot(rand(1,10))
nexttile; histogram(randn(1,300))
nexttile([1 2]); plot(cumsum(randn(1,200)))
title(t, 'Overview')
xlabel(t, 'sample')
tools.notes: Available since R2019b. A 'flow' layout rearranges tiles as the figure resizes, which is convenient when the number of panels is data dependent. Nested layouts are created by passing a tile as the parent.

tools.name: nexttile
tools.description: Creates the next axes in a tiled chart layout and makes it current, optionally at a specific tile index or spanning several tiles. Use it after `tiledlayout` in place of repeated `subplot` calls. It returns the axes handle so plots can be directed explicitly.
tools.usage:
nexttile
nexttile(tileNum)
nexttile(span)
nexttile(tileNum, span)
ax = nexttile(___)

parameters.name: tileNum
parameters.description: Index of the tile to use.

parameters.name: span
parameters.description: Two-element [r c] giving how many rows and columns to span.

parameters.name: 'north', 'south', 'east', 'west'
parameters.description: Place the axes outside the grid on that side.

tools.notes: Spanning tiles must not overlap already-created tiles. Capturing the axes handle and passing it to plotting functions keeps code clear when many tiles are involved.

tools.name: hold
tools.description: Controls whether new plots add to the current axes or replace its contents. `hold on` keeps existing graphics and preserves axis limits and the colour order index; `hold off` restores the default replace behaviour. Use it to overlay several data series on one set of axes.
tools.usage:
hold on
hold off
hold all
hold(ax, 'on')
hold

parameters.name: ax
parameters.description: Axes to operate on; the current axes by default.

parameters.name: 'on'/'off'
parameters.description: Enable or disable retention of existing plots.

tools.example:
x = linspace(0, 2*pi, 100);
plot(x, sin(x))
hold on
plot(x, cos(x))
plot(x, sin(2*x))
hold off
legend('sin','cos','sin2')
ax = gca; hold(ax, 'on');
tools.notes: Forgetting `hold off` in a function leaves the axes in a modified state for later code; specify the axes explicitly or restore the state. Calling `hold` with no argument toggles the current setting.

tools.name: grid
tools.description: Turns grid lines on or off for the current axes, with `grid minor` adding lines at the minor ticks. Use it to make values easier to read off a plot, especially on logarithmic axes. Per-axis control is available through the axes XGrid, YGrid and ZGrid properties.
tools.usage:
grid on
grid off
grid minor
grid(ax, 'on')
grid
tools.notes: GridAlpha, GridColor and GridLineStyle on the axes object give finer control than the on/off command. Minor grid lines are essential for reading logarithmic axes accurately.

tools.name: axis
tools.description: Sets axis limits and controls aspect ratio, visibility and scaling mode with a single command. Options such as 'equal', 'tight', 'square' and 'image' cover the common cases that would otherwise need several property assignments. Use it to make circles look circular and to trim white space around data.
tools.usage:
axis([xmin xmax ymin ymax])
axis([xmin xmax ymin ymax zmin zmax])
axis style
axis(ax, ___)
limits = axis
tools.example:
t = linspace(0, 2*pi, 200);
plot(cos(t), sin(t))
axis equal
axis([-1.5 1.5 -1.5 1.5])
limits = axis
imagesc(peaks(50)); axis image off
tools.notes: Without `axis equal`, a circle plots as an ellipse whenever the axes box is not square. `axis tight` removes padding while `axis padded` (R2021a and later) adds a small margin instead.

tools.name: xlim
tools.description: Sets or queries the x-axis limits, or switches between automatic and manual limit modes. Passing a two-element vector fixes the limits, and passing 'auto' lets MATLAB choose again. Use it to zoom into a region of interest and to make several plots share the same scale.
tools.usage:
xlim(limits)
xl = xlim
xlim('auto')
xlim('manual')
xlim(ax, ___)
xlim('padded')
xlim('tight')

parameters.name: limits
parameters.description: Two-element increasing vector, which may contain -Inf or Inf to leave one end automatic.

tools.example:
plot(linspace(0, 100, 1000), cumsum(randn(1,1000)))
xlim([20 60])
xl = xlim
xlim('auto')
xlim([0 Inf])
ylim([-10 10]); zlim auto
tools.notes: Using Inf or -Inf as one limit keeps that end automatic, which is useful for anchoring an axis at zero. `ylim` and `zlim` behave identically for the other axes.

tools.name: ylim
tools.description: Sets or queries the y-axis limits or limit mode. Use it to align the vertical scale across subplots, to clip extreme outliers from view, and to anchor a bar chart baseline at zero. It accepts the same 'auto', 'manual', 'tight' and 'padded' modes as `xlim`.
tools.usage:
ylim(limits)
yl = ylim
ylim('auto')
ylim(ax, ___)

parameters.name: limits
parameters.description: Two-element increasing vector, possibly with Inf.

tools.notes: `linkaxes` keeps limits synchronized as you zoom, which is better than setting them by hand on every panel. Setting a limit switches that axis to manual mode until you set it back to 'auto'.

tools.name: zlim
tools.description: Sets or queries the z-axis limits of 3-D axes, with the same modes as `xlim` and `ylim`. Use it to clip a surface vertically, to standardize the height scale across several 3-D plots, and to position the contours drawn by `surfc` beneath a surface. It has no effect on 2-D axes.
tools.usage:
zlim(limits)
zl = zlim
zlim('auto')
zlim(ax, ___)
tools.example:
[X, Y] = meshgrid(linspace(-3, 3, 60));
surf(X, Y, peaks(X, Y), 'EdgeColor', 'none')
zlim([-5 5])
zl = zlim
view(-40, 30)
tools.notes: Clipping with zlim hides surface regions outside the range rather than compressing them; set the data to NaN if you want holes instead of flat clipping.

tools.name: xticks
tools.description: Sets or queries the x-axis tick locations, or switches the tick mode to automatic. Use it to place ticks at meaningful values such as integers, multiples of pi or category boundaries. `yticks` and `zticks` do the same for the other axes.
tools.usage:
xticks(ticks)
xt = xticks
xticks('auto')
xticks('manual')
xticks(ax, ___)
tools.example:
x = linspace(0, 2*pi, 200);
plot(x, sin(x))
xticks(0:pi/2:2*pi)
xticklabels({'0','\pi/2','\pi','3\pi/2','2\pi'})
xt = xticks
yticks(-1:0.5:1)
tools.notes: Setting ticks switches TickMode to manual, so ticks no longer adapt when you zoom. Tick values outside the axis limits are simply not drawn.

tools.name: xticklabels
tools.description: Sets or queries the text shown at each x tick, independently of the tick positions. Use it for custom units, category names, TeX symbols and rotated labels. Set the labels after the ticks, because changing tick locations resets the labels to automatic.
tools.usage:
xticklabels(labels)
xtl = xticklabels
xticklabels('auto')
xticklabels('manual')
xticklabels(ax, ___)

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: Cell array or string array of labels, one per tick.

tools.notes: If there are fewer labels than ticks, MATLAB cycles through them, which produces confusing repeats. `xtickangle` rotates long labels so they do not overlap.

tools.name: xlabel
tools.description: Adds or replaces the x-axis label, with support for TeX and LaTeX markup and full text property control. Use it to state the quantity and its units, which is the single most valuable annotation on any plot. It returns the Text object for later modification.
tools.usage:
xlabel(txt)
xlabel(ax, txt)
xlabel(___, Name, Value)
t = xlabel(___)

parameters.name: txt
parameters.description: Label text; supports TeX by default.

tools.notes: Underscores in a TeX-interpreted label create subscripts, so set Interpreter to 'none' for literal variable or file names. For tiled layouts, `xlabel(t, ...)` on the layout labels all tiles at once.

tools.name: ylabel
tools.description: Adds or replaces the y-axis label with the same options as `xlabel`. For axes with two y axes, use `yyaxis left` or `yyaxis right` first to choose which side you are labelling. Always include units where they exist.
tools.usage:
ylabel(txt)
ylabel(ax, txt)
ylabel(___, Name, Value)
t = ylabel(___)

parameters.name: 'FontSize', 'Rotation'
parameters.description: Text appearance; Rotation 0 makes a horizontal label.

tools.example:
yyaxis left
plot(1:10, rand(1,10))
ylabel('pressure (kPa)')
yyaxis right
plot(1:10, 100*rand(1,10))
ylabel('temperature (\circC)')
xlabel('sample')
tools.notes: A long vertical label is hard to read; `'Rotation', 0` with extra horizontal padding is a common alternative. With `yyaxis`, each side has its own label, colour order and limits.

tools.name: zlabel
tools.description: Adds or replaces the z-axis label on 3-D axes, with the same text options as the other label functions. Use it on surface, mesh and 3-D scatter plots where the vertical quantity needs naming. It has no visible effect on 2-D axes.
tools.usage:
zlabel(txt)
zlabel(ax, txt)
zlabel(___, Name, Value)
t = zlabel(___)
tools.example:
[X, Y] = meshgrid(linspace(-2, 2, 40));
surf(X, Y, X.^2 - Y.^2, 'EdgeColor', 'none')
xlabel('x'); ylabel('y'); zlabel('z = x^2 - y^2')
view(-35, 30)
colorbar
tools.notes: The z label rotates with the view, so choose a viewpoint where it remains legible. TeX markup such as ^2 works by default.

tools.name: title
tools.description: Adds a title above the axes, with an optional subtitle since R2020b. Use it to state what the plot shows, including key parameters. Titles accept TeX and LaTeX markup and all standard text properties.
tools.usage:
title(txt)
title(txt, subtxt)
title(ax, ___)
title(___, Name, Value)
[t, s] = title(___)

parameters.name: txt
parameters.description: Title text; a cell array gives a multi-line title.

tools.notes: For a title spanning all panels of a tiled layout use `title(t, ...)` on the layout object, or `sgtitle` for a subplot grid. A cell array of character vectors creates multiple lines.

tools.name: sgtitle
tools.description: Adds a title centred above a grid of subplots in a figure. Use it to give a name to a whole multi-panel figure created with `subplot`. For tiled chart layouts, call `title` on the layout object instead.
tools.usage:
sgtitle(txt)
sgtitle(target, txt)
sgtitle(___, Name, Value)
sg = sgtitle(___)

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: Figure or panel containing the subplots.

tools.example:
figure
subplot(2,2,1); plot(rand(1,10)); title('a')
subplot(2,2,2); plot(rand(1,10)); title('b')
subplot(2,2,3); plot(rand(1,10)); title('c')
subplot(2,2,4); plot(rand(1,10)); title('d')
sgtitle('Experiment 3 summary', 'FontSize', 14, 'FontWeight', 'bold')
tools.notes: Available since R2018b. It reserves space at the top of the figure, which can crowd the first row of subplots; adjust with `tiledlayout` padding or figure size.

tools.name: legend
tools.description: Creates a legend describing the plotted series, taking labels from the arguments or from each object's DisplayName property. Location and orientation options place it inside or outside the axes. Use it whenever more than one series shares an axes.
tools.usage:
legend
legend(labels)
legend(subset, labels)
legend('Location', loc)
legend('off')
lgd = legend(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: Cell array or string array of labels in plotting order.

parameters.name: 'AutoUpdate'
parameters.description: 'on' (default) or 'off' to freeze the legend as new series are added.

tools.notes: Set 'HandleVisibility' to 'off' on reference lines so they are excluded from the legend, or turn 'AutoUpdate' off. Using DisplayName on each plot keeps labels attached to the right series when the plotting order changes.

tools.name: colorbar
tools.description: Adds a colour scale bar to the axes, showing how colours map to data values. Location, tick positions, tick labels and a label string are all configurable. Use it on every plot where colour encodes a quantity, otherwise the colours are uninterpretable.
tools.usage:
colorbar
colorbar(location)
c = colorbar(___, Name, Value)
colorbar('off')
colorbar(ax, ___)
tools.notes: The colorbar reflects the current colour limits, so call `clim` before or after and it updates. Colorbars steal space from the axes; in tiled layouts attach one to the layout to share it across tiles.

tools.name: colormap
tools.description: Sets or queries the colormap of a figure or axes, from a built-in map name, a function returning an n-by-3 matrix, or an explicit RGB matrix. Use it to choose a perceptually uniform map for scientific data and a diverging map for signed quantities. Since R2019b colormaps can be set per axes rather than per figure.
tools.usage:
colormap(map)
colormap(target, map)
cmap = colormap
colormap(map(n))

parameters.name: map
parameters.description: Name such as parula, turbo, gray, hot, jet, cool, copper, sky, or an n-by-3 RGB matrix.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of colours when calling a colormap function.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: Figure or axes to apply the map to.

tools.example:
imagesc(peaks(60))
colormap(turbo)
colorbar
ax = gca;
colormap(ax, gray(16))
custom = [linspace(0,1,64)' zeros(64,1) linspace(1,0,64)'];
colormap(custom)
tools.notes: Avoid jet for scientific data: it is not perceptually uniform and creates false structure. parula, turbo, viridis-like and the diverging maps are better choices, and greyscale is safest for printing.

tools.name: clim
tools.description: Sets or queries the colour limits that map data values onto the colormap, formerly named `caxis`. Use it to fix a common colour scale across several plots and to centre a diverging colormap on zero. Values outside the limits are clamped to the end colours.
tools.usage:
clim(limits)
cl = clim
clim('auto')
clim('manual')
clim(ax, ___)
tools.example:
Z = peaks(50);
tiledlayout(1,2)
nexttile; imagesc(Z); clim([-8 8]); colorbar
nexttile; imagesc(2*Z); clim([-8 8]); colorbar
colormap(turbo)
cl = clim
tools.notes: Renamed from `caxis` in R2022a; `caxis` still works but is not recommended for new code. Setting symmetric limits around zero is essential for diverging colormaps to read correctly.

tools.name: view
tools.description: Sets or queries the viewpoint of 3-D axes as an azimuth and elevation pair, or from a direction vector. Use it to choose a readable angle for surfaces, to create rotating animations, and to switch quickly between plan and oblique views. view(2) and view(3) select the standard 2-D and 3-D viewpoints.
tools.usage:
view(az, el)
view([az el])
view([x y z])
view(2)
view(3)
[az, el] = view

parameters.name: az
parameters.description: Azimuth in degrees, rotation about the z axis.

parameters.name: el
parameters.description: Elevation in degrees above the xy plane.

tools.example:
[X, Y] = meshgrid(linspace(-3,3,50));
surf(X, Y, peaks(X, Y), 'EdgeColor', 'none')
view(3)
for az = -180:10:180
    view(az, 30); drawnow limitrate
end
[az, el] = view
tools.notes: view(2) looks straight down, which turns a surface into a filled contour-like image. For fixed aspect during rotation, combine with `axis vis3d` so the box does not resize.

tools.name: camlight
tools.description: Creates or moves a light object positioned relative to the camera, which makes 3-D surfaces look solid rather than flat. Use it together with `lighting` and `material` to give depth to surface and patch plots. Repositioning an existing light keeps it attached as the view changes.
tools.usage:
camlight
camlight(kind)
camlight(az, el)
camlight(lightHandle, ___)
lgt = camlight(___)

parameters.name: az, el
parameters.description: Azimuth and elevation relative to the camera.

tools.notes: Lights do not follow the camera automatically, so call camlight again after changing the view or the shading will look wrong. Too many lights wash out the surface; one or two is usually enough.

tools.name: lighting
tools.description: Selects the lighting algorithm used to shade surfaces and patches: flat per face, gouraud interpolated across vertices, or none. Gouraud produces smooth shading and is the usual choice for continuous surfaces. Use it after adding a light with `camlight` or `light`.
tools.usage:
lighting flat
lighting gouraud
lighting none
lighting(ax, style)
tools.example:
[X, Y, Z] = sphere(60);
surf(X, Y, Z, 'EdgeColor', 'none')
axis equal
camlight
lighting gouraud
material shiny
lighting flat
tools.notes: Lighting has no visible effect until at least one light object exists in the axes. The older 'phong' option was removed; gouraud is the smooth alternative.

tools.name: shading
tools.description: Sets the colour shading mode of surface and patch objects: faceted with visible mesh lines, flat with one colour per face and no lines, or interp with colours interpolated across each face. Use 'interp' for smooth continuous fields and 'faceted' when the grid structure matters. It is a shorthand for setting the FaceColor and EdgeColor properties.
tools.usage:
shading faceted
shading flat
shading interp
shading(ax, style)
tools.notes: On dense grids the default faceted mode turns the surface black with mesh lines; flat or interp is almost always better. `shading interp` is equivalent to setting FaceColor to 'interp' and EdgeColor to 'none'.

tools.name: set
tools.description: Sets one or more properties on one or more graphics objects, accepting arrays of handles so that a whole group can be changed at once. Called with no value it lists the allowed values for a property. Modern code often uses dot notation instead, but `set` remains the way to change many objects in one call.
tools.usage:
set(H, Name, Value)
set(H, Name1, Value1, ..., NameN, ValueN)
set(H, S)
values = set(H, Name)

parameters.name: H
parameters.description: Graphics object handle or array of handles.

parameters.name: S
parameters.description: Structure whose fields are property names.

tools.example:
h = plot(rand(5, 3));
set(h, 'LineWidth', 1.5)
set(h, {'Color'}, {[1 0 0]; [0 1 0]; [0 0 1]})
set(gca, 'FontSize', 12, 'Box', 'off')
set(groot, 'defaultAxesFontSize', 12)
set(gca, 'YScale')
tools.notes: Passing a cell array of property names and a matching cell of values assigns different values to each handle. Setting defaults on `groot` applies to every figure created afterwards in the session.

tools.name: get
tools.description: Queries property values of graphics objects, returning a single value, a structure of all properties, or a cell array for arrays of handles. Use it to inspect what a plotting function created and to read current limits, colours and data. Dot notation is more readable for a single object, but get works uniformly over handle arrays.
tools.usage:
v = get(H, Name)
S = get(H)
v = get(H, {Name1, Name2})
values = get(groot, 'factory')

parameters.name: Name
parameters.description: Property name or cell array of names.

tools.notes: `get(H)` on a complex object returns a very large structure; use `properties(H)` to list names only. For a single object, dot access such as `h.Color` is both faster and clearer.

tools.name: gca
tools.description: Returns the handle of the current axes, creating one in the current figure if none exists. Use it to adjust properties of the axes that a plotting function just drew into. Storing handles explicitly is more robust than relying on gca in functions and callbacks.
tools.usage:
ax = gca
ax = gca(fig)

parameters.name: fig
parameters.description: Figure whose current axes is returned.

tools.notes: gca creates an axes as a side effect if none exists, which can produce stray empty figures in scripts. Capture handles from the plotting call instead when the code may run with other figures open.

tools.name: gcf
tools.description: Returns the handle of the current figure, creating one if none exists. Use it to set figure-level properties such as size, colour and renderer, and to pass the figure to export functions. As with `gca`, explicit handles are preferable inside functions.
tools.usage: fig = gcf
tools.notes: `gco` returns the most recently clicked object, which is useful in interactive callbacks. `groot` is the root object holding session-wide graphics defaults.

tools.name: findobj
tools.description: Searches the graphics object hierarchy for objects matching property values, returning an array of handles. Use it to find all lines in a figure, all axes with a given tag, or objects created by code you did not write. Tagging objects at creation makes them easy to find later.
tools.usage:
h = findobj
h = findobj(Name, Value)
h = findobj(objhandles, Name, Value)
h = findobj(___, '-regexp', Name, Expr)
h = findall(___)

parameters.name: '-regexp'
parameters.description: Match property values with a regular expression.

parameters.name: '-depth', d
parameters.description: Limit search depth in the hierarchy.

tools.notes: `findobj` skips objects with HandleVisibility set to 'off', while `findall` includes them, which is why findall is needed to restyle legends and colorbars. Setting a Tag at creation is the reliable way to locate objects later.

tools.name: annotation
tools.description: Adds arrows, lines, boxes, ellipses and text boxes positioned in normalized figure coordinates rather than data coordinates. Use it for callouts, brackets and notes that should stay put regardless of the data limits. Positions are given as [x y width height] with (0,0) at the bottom left of the figure.
tools.usage:
annotation(lineType, x, y)
annotation(shapeType, dim)
annotation(___, Name, Value)
an = annotation(___)

parameters.name: x, y
parameters.description: Two-element normalized start and end coordinates for line types.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: [x y w h] normalized position for shape types.

tools.example:
plot(linspace(0,10,200), sin(linspace(0,10,200)))
annotation('textarrow', [0.4 0.32], [0.8 0.68], 'String', 'first peak')
annotation('rectangle', [0.15 0.15 0.2 0.3], 'Color', 'r', 'LineWidth', 1.5)
annotation('textbox', [0.6 0.7 0.25 0.15], 'String', 'note', 'FitBoxToText', 'on')
tools.notes: Because coordinates are normalized to the figure, annotations do not move with the data when you zoom or change limits; use `text` for data-anchored labels. Resizing the figure rescales annotation positions proportionally.

tools.name: saveas
tools.description: Saves a figure to a file in a chosen format, inferred from the extension or given explicitly. It captures the whole figure including all axes and annotations. For publication-quality output with tight cropping, `exportgraphics` generally gives better results.
tools.usage:
saveas(fig, filename)
saveas(fig, filename, formattype)

parameters.name: fig
parameters.description: Figure or other graphics object handle.

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: Output file name; the extension selects the format.

tools.example:
plot(1:10, rand(1,10))
saveas(gcf, 'plot.png')
saveas(gcf, 'plot.pdf')
saveas(gcf, 'plot', 'epsc')
saveas(gcf, 'plot.fig')
tools.notes: saveas pads the output with the figure's white margins and uses screen resolution for bitmaps. `exportgraphics` crops tightly and accepts a Resolution option, and `print` gives the most control over renderers and paper size.

tools.name: exportgraphics
tools.description: Exports a figure, axes, tiled layout or chart to an image or document file with tight cropping and explicit control over resolution, background colour and vector versus image content. It is the recommended way to produce figures for papers, reports and slides. Appending to a PDF builds a multi-page document.
tools.usage:
exportgraphics(obj, filename)
exportgraphics(obj, filename, Name, Value)

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: Figure, axes, tiled layout or chart object to export.

parameters.name: 'Resolution'
parameters.description: Dots per inch for image formats; 150 by default.

parameters.name: 'ContentType'
parameters.description: 'auto', 'vector' or 'image' for PDF and EPS output.

parameters.name: 'Append'
parameters.description: true to add a page to an existing PDF.

tools.example:
f = figure('Visible', 'off');
plot(linspace(0,10,200), sin(linspace(0,10,200)))
exportgraphics(f, 'fig1.png', 'Resolution', 300)
exportgraphics(f, 'fig1.pdf', 'ContentType', 'vector')
exportgraphics(gca, 'axes_only.png', 'BackgroundColor', 'none')
close(f)
tools.notes: Available since R2020a. Exporting an axes rather than the figure omits other panels and surrounding white space. Transparent backgrounds are supported for PNG but not for JPEG.

tools.name: print
tools.description: Prints a figure to a printer or writes it to a file, with the widest set of options for renderers, resolution, paper handling and vector formats. Use it when you need painters versus opengl rendering control or specific EPS and PDF behaviour. The driver string selects the output format.
tools.usage:
print(filename, formattype)
print(fig, filename, formattype)
print(___, '-r300')
print(___, '-painters')
cdata = print('-RGBImage')

parameters.name: '-r<dpi>'
parameters.description: Output resolution in dots per inch.

parameters.name: '-painters'/'-opengl'
parameters.description: Renderer: painters for clean vector output, opengl for transparency and lighting.

parameters.name: '-RGBImage'
parameters.description: Return the rendered figure as an image array instead of writing a file.

tools.example:
plot(1:10, rand(1,10))
print('plot300', '-dpng', '-r300')
print(gcf, 'vector', '-depsc', '-painters')
img = print('-RGBImage', '-r150');
size(img)
tools.notes: The painters renderer produces true vector output but cannot render transparency or complex lighting; opengl rasterizes those parts. For most modern workflows `exportgraphics` is simpler and crops better.

tools.name: savefig
tools.description: Saves one or more figures to a .fig file that preserves the complete graphics object hierarchy and the underlying data. Reopening the file gives a fully interactive, editable figure. Use it to archive results you may need to re-examine, rescale or restyle later.
tools.usage:
savefig(filename)
savefig(H, filename)
savefig(H, filename, 'compact')

parameters.name: H
parameters.description: Figure handle or array of handles to save.

parameters.name: 'compact'
parameters.description: Save a smaller file that cannot be opened in releases before R2014b.

tools.example:
plot(linspace(0,10,200), sin(linspace(0,10,200)))
savefig('result.fig')
savefig([f1 f2], 'both.fig')
close all
openfig('result.fig');
tools.notes: A .fig file embeds all the plotted data, so it can be large and it also means the data is recoverable from the file. It is not a portable image format; export to PNG or PDF for sharing.

tools.name: openfig
tools.description: Opens a saved .fig file and returns the figure handle, optionally reusing an already-open copy or opening it invisibly. Use it to reload archived figures for restyling, for extracting data from old plots, and for building report pipelines. Combine with `findobj` to pull XData and YData back out.
tools.usage:
fig = openfig(filename)
fig = openfig(filename, copies)
fig = openfig(filename, visibility)
fig = openfig(filename, copies, visibility)
tools.notes: Opening invisibly and exporting is the standard way to regenerate images from archived figures in a batch job. Figures saved in much newer releases may not open in older ones.

tools.name: close
tools.description: Closes figure windows by handle, number, name, or all at once. Use it to clean up after generating figures in a loop and to keep memory use under control in long batch runs. The 'force' option closes figures whose CloseRequestFcn would otherwise block.
tools.usage:
close
close(fig)
close all
close all hidden
close(fig, 'force')
status = close(___)

parameters.name: 'hidden'
parameters.description: Also close figures with hidden handles.

tools.notes: Figures created in a loop without closing them accumulate and eventually exhaust memory. `close all hidden` is needed for figures created by apps and tools that hide their handles.

tools.name: clf
tools.description: Clears the current figure by deleting its children, leaving the window itself open. Use it at the start of a plotting routine to guarantee a clean canvas without the flicker of closing and recreating a window. The 'reset' option also restores figure properties to their defaults.
tools.usage:
clf
clf('reset')
clf(fig)
clf(fig, 'reset')
fig = clf(___)

parameters.name: 'reset'
parameters.description: Also reset figure properties, except Position, Units, PaperPosition and PaperUnits.

tools.notes: Plain `clf` leaves figure properties such as Colormap and Color in place, which is usually what you want inside an update loop. `cla` clears a single axes and `cla reset` also restores its properties.

tools.name: drawnow
tools.description: Flushes the graphics event queue so that pending plot updates are rendered and callbacks are processed. Use it in animation and progress-display loops where MATLAB would otherwise defer drawing until the loop ends. The 'limitrate' option skips frames to keep loops fast.
tools.usage:
drawnow
drawnow limitrate
drawnow nocallbacks
drawnow limitrate nocallbacks

parameters.name: 'limitrate'
parameters.description: Update at most about 20 times per second, dropping intermediate frames.

parameters.name: 'nocallbacks'
parameters.description: Defer callbacks, preventing interruption of the running code.

parameters.name: 'expose'
parameters.description: Update graphics without processing callbacks or the queue.

tools.notes: A bare `drawnow` in a tight loop dominates the run time; 'limitrate' typically makes animations several times faster with no visible difference. Updating XData and YData of an existing object is far faster than replotting.
